summary: The RMAC pipeline is operationally mature—daily push-forward runs reliably, 10 problems carry best proofs, and a 26% resolution rate shows the discover→resolve loop is producing movement. However, the system has a critical verification gap (0/10 proofs verified) and is dangerously homogeneous in model and methodology, meaning it can generate proofs at scale but cannot yet certify them, and shares a single model's blind spots across every agent.
problems: Zero verified proofs (0/10): the pipeline produces and scores proofs but has no closed-loop formal/independent verification, so 'best proof' status is self-reported quality, not correctness.
Meeting/discussion system is entirely unused (0 rooms, 0 messages) despite being a defined pipeline stage—either it provides no value, is too costly to trigger, or is silently failing to launch.

Severe model monoculture: all agents (critic, solver, evaluator, meeting) and proof generation run on the same Claude-subscription backend, so the evaluator shares the solver's blind spots and cannot catch errors the generator is systematically prone to.

Solvability-evaluator and critic are likely correlated: an LLM scoring proofs 0-100% that came from a sibling LLM tends toward generous, self-consistent scores—no calibration against ground-truth or human spot-checks is described.

Observability is thin: today shows 0 runs/0 cost while cumulative is $78.55/27 runs, suggesting per-agent tracing, failure logging, and 'why did this agent stall' diagnostics are not surfaced to engineers.
Issue-based evaluation can be gamed by the loop: the same family of agents discovers issues and resolves them, so resolution rate measures internal agreement rather than external proof validity.
highlights: Push-forward automation is robust and consistent—13 daily runs completed with a current last-run date, indicating the core orchestration is stable.
Clean separation of concerns across agents (critic discovers, solver resolves, evaluator scores) is a sound architectural foundation that supports adding diversity and verification layers.
Local tectonic LaTeX compilation and per-problem JSON+.tex proof storage give a reproducible, inspectable artifact trail.
Resource cost is modest ($78.55 cumulative over 27 runs), leaving ample budget headroom to invest in cross-model verification and adversarial review without major spend concerns.

suggested_todos.title: Add a cross-model verifier: route every best proof through a second, different model family (or formal/proof-checker tooling) before it can reach 'verified'; gate the verified count on independent confirmation
Decouple evaluator from generator—run solvability scoring on a distinct model and periodically calibrate scores against a small human-audited gold set to detect score inflation
Diagnose and either fix or retire the meeting system: instrument room-creation triggers, log failures, and run a controlled A/B on whether persona discussion improves resolution vs. cost
Build per-agent observability: structured run logs, stall/timeout detection, token-and-cost attribution per agent, and an alert when an agent produces empty or malformed output
Introduce an adversarial 'kill-argument' review stage between resolve and eval so the strongest rejection of each proof is generated before scoring
Add model/strategy diversity to the solver: maintain a small ensemble (different model families or prompting strategies) and compare proof attempts rather than relying on one backend
Define and track a ground-truth-anchored benchmark metric (e.g., agreement with human verdicts on a held-out set) separate from internal resolution rate
Automate regression detection: when a new daily run lowers a proof's score or reopens a resolved issue, flag it for engineer review instead of silently overwriting

mistakes: Treating a self-generated solvability score as a proxy for correctness—the system optimizes for what its own evaluator rewards, not for verifiable truth.
Defining pipeline stages (meeting discussion) that are never exercised, creating dead architecture that masks whether the documented pipeline reflects reality.
Single-model dependency across discovery, resolution, and evaluation, which collapses the independence that makes multi-agent review meaningful.
Measuring throughput (runs, issues resolved, proofs produced) far more thoroughly than measuring correctness, so the dashboard looks healthy while the verification rate sits at zero.
Letting the same agent family both create and close issues, turning the resolution rate into a measure of internal consensus rather than external validity.
Insufficient failure-mode visibility: with no per-agent error logging surfaced, a silently degrading agent could continue running daily without anyone noticing until output quality drops.
